artifacts.title: Biese et al. v. Tennessee Valley Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: Biese and others complained that Tennessee Valley Presbytery erred by approving Redeemer Church session minutes without exception—minutes noting a youth Super Bowl party—and by denying their complaint seeking a Sabbath exception. The SJC denied the complaint: because Presbytery gave no reasons for its actions, the record was insufficient to find it erred in interpreting the Constitution. A concurrence said the denial did not decide the Sabbath merits; a dissent would have held the complaint judicially out of order for lack of SJC jurisdiction over presbytery record review.

artifacts.title: Herron et al. v. Central Indiana Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: Herron and others challenged Presbytery’s decision to proceed to trial after a BCO 31-2 finding, his administrative suspension, denial of access to Presbytery records and meetings, and a public statement. The SJC sustained only the access issue: suspension from official functions did not remove his membership rights, though it did not entitle him to every investigative-committee document. Finding no clear error on the other issues, it ordered trial to proceed, temporarily stayed censure decisions, and postponed related complaints through trial and any appeal.

artifacts.title: Eagle v. Savannah River Presbytery

The SJC held the complaint administratively out of order as prematurely filed and did not reach the merits. It reset the complainant's time to elevate the complaint so that timing begins on the later of notification of the SJC action or Presbytery's ruling. The SJC adopted the decision by roll call.

artifacts.synopsis: A member removed from the rolls under BCO 38-4 challenged Presbytery's ruling that she lacked standing to complain because she was no longer a member. The SJC sustained the complaint: standing under BCO 43-1 cannot be defeated by the very removal challenged. Removal under BCO 38-4 is pastoral discipline, a disciplinary case, not a merely administrative act. The SJC remanded to Presbytery to consider the complaint and take the action it should have taken—remand to the Session. The merits of the removal were not decided.

artifacts.title: Yoo et al. v. Korean Southwest Orange County Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: The SJC found the complaint administratively out of order and dismissed it. The complainants had not documented that they first presented the complaint to Korean Southwest Orange County Presbytery under BCO 43-2, and the SJC held that the Presbytery—not the SJC—was the proper court for the charges and specifications in the March 2, 2020 letter. The dismissal was recorded 19-0-0; no merits were reached.

artifacts.title: Mapes v. Metropolitan New York Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: A complaint sought a congregational meeting to vote on leaving the PCA after the temporary session denied the request in November 2017. The SJC dismissed the complaint as moot and not judicially in order. Both parties agreed at the panel hearing that the presbytery had voted in October 2018 to dismiss the congregation pending consent under BCO 13-9(f), and consent was given at a December 2018 called meeting. No merits ruling was made. Three commissioners dissented; one was disqualified.

artifacts.synopsis: Heritage Presbytery treated a member's September 2016 filing against her session as a BCO 43-3 complaint and began adjudicating it. The SJC sustained RE Scott Dailey's complaint against that action. BCO 43-3 allows higher-court review only if the lower court denies a complaint or fails to consider it by its next stated meeting. Presbytery's post-November 12, 2016 adjudicative actions were annulled; possible underlying disciplinary matters were left to BCO 31-2 and 40-5.

artifacts.title: Aven v. Ohio Valley Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: An SJC complaint alleged that Ohio Valley Presbytery failed to comply with the SJC's prior remand in Case 2014-01, which required it to 'hear further' from TE Charles Hickey about his changed view on Larger Catechism 177. The SJC denied the complaint. It held that the prior decision neither sustained nor denied the original complaint and prescribed no particular examination procedure; Hickey's nine pages of additional affirmations, exegesis, and answers constituted hearing further, and he addressed the five identified areas at least in part. A concurrence believed the SJC could also have adjudicated the confessional-difference merits; a dissent would have found noncompliance and reached the merits.

artifacts.synopsis: The SJC found TE Arnold Robertstad's complaint against North Texas Presbytery administratively out of order and incapable of being put in order under BCO 43-3. Robertstad initially filed by e-mail—not an allowed filing—and his hard-copy filing arrived after the thirty-day deadline. The SJC reasoned that BCO 42-4/43-3 notification language concerns a lower court notifying parties, not party e-filing, and OMSJC 18.10.b bars e-mail filing. The merits were not reached; a concurrence urged later clarification by amendment, and no further proceedings are indicated.

artifacts.title: Wills v. Metro Atlanta Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: Did a presbytery violate the BCO or clearly err by dissolving a congregation without its consent? The SJC said no and denied the complaint. On the constitutional issue, it held that BCO 13-9.f grants dissolution power and BCO 40-6 does not impose formal process for it. On the discretionary issue, it found no clear error in the record. The denial left dissolution in place and warned that such action still requires sufficient justification and prudent, reviewable procedure.

artifacts.title: Aven and Dively v. Ohio Valley Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: Two ministers complained that Ohio Valley Presbytery erred by judging TE Charles Hickey's difference with Larger Catechism 177—over restricting the Lord's Supper to those able to examine themselves—as more than semantic but neither hostile to the system nor vital to religion. The SJC neither sustained nor denied the complaint. Because the Record did not sufficiently address Hickey's particular expression and rationale, the Commission remanded to Presbytery for further hearing and a fuller record. It reserved the merits, including whether this formulation of paedocommunion is allowable.

artifacts.synopsis: After a Session excommunicated a member without trial for contumacy, the SJC sustained his complaint and annulled the contumacy judgment, excommunication, and later Session and Presbytery actions. No mutually agreed BCO 38-1 confession existed, and declining a confession meeting was not immediately censurable objective contumacy under BCO 32-6; subjective contumacy required confession or trial. He reverted to membership under pending indictment. The SJC did not find the indictment unconstitutional, decide trial guilt, or consider the unpleaded trespass warning.

artifacts.synopsis: The SJC sustained the Session's complaint against Presbytery. Presbytery had ruled a member's original complaint administratively out of order as untimely but then remanded the matter to the Session; the SJC held that once out of order, no complaint remained to remand. It also held Presbytery could not direct or instruct the Session to initiate formal process without BCO 40-5's required citation step, so those directions were null and void. The member remained under the Session's jurisdiction; the civil trespass order was not ecclesiastical discipline and did not alter membership.

artifacts.synopsis: Sherfey challenged James River Presbytery’s denial of his complaint and alleged errors in its commission’s proceedings. Incorrect advice from Presbytery’s clerk did not excuse compliance. The adopted decision neither reached the merits nor ordered a remand; only a concurrence proposed returning the matter to Presbytery.

It reached no merits. The dissent argued rescission did not automatically defeat a complaint and that her complaint also alleged Presbytery’s failure to act.

artifacts.synopsis: Black challenged Presbytery’s handling of his complaint and its ruling that a licentiate’s non-24-hour creation-day view was not an exception to the Westminster Standards. The SJC denied remand because Presbytery had effectively adjudicated the complaint; the separate objection to proceeding without Black was not first filed below and was administratively out of order. It upheld Presbytery’s ruling that not every non-Calendar-Day view constitutes an exception. artifacts.synopsis: Smith complained that Northeast Presbytery failed to provide pastoral care after dissolving Grace Presbyterian Church. The SJC rejected Presbytery's objections that the complaint lacked supporting reasons or was barred by Smith's protest, held it in order, but denied it on the merits. Distinguishing the pastoral 'power of order' from judicial 'power of jurisdiction,' the SJC ruled that the Constitution neither requires nor permits a presbytery to retain jurisdiction over individual members of a dissolved particular church, and that pastoral care of former members is generally discretionary; on these facts, Presbytery's efforts satisfied any duty.

artifacts.synopsis: The SJC denied Hopper's complaint against James River Presbytery's April 13, 1991 order barring him from teaching or preaching his views on prophecy and tongues. It rejected all five specifications: Scripture did not forbid the order; the 1974 Pastoral Letter did not address presbytery's power to enjoin such teaching; forbearance did not preclude protecting peace and purity; presbytery could restrict preaching short of a heresy finding without binding conscience; and allowing presbyteral discussion while restricting congregational teaching was not inconsistent. The action remained in force.
